title: Walks in Ashcombe Vale: the Ashcombe Beacon loop and more | Sample Outdoors
meta description: The Ashcombe Beacon loop: 9.5 km, 310 m of ascent, with parking, cafés and dog advice.
body:
Planning a walk near Ashcombe Vale? Sample Outdoors has put together this guide to walking in and around the area, with routes for every ability. Before you set off, check the weather forecast, wear supportive footwear and carry water, a map and a charged phone.

The Ashcombe Beacon loop

The Ashcombe Beacon loop is a 9.5 km circular walk with 310 metres of ascent, starting from the village hall car park on Mill Lane (pay and display, 40 spaces). Grassy bridleways give way to a stony climb onto the beacon, where the path can be boggy after rain. Highlights include the ruined signal tower and views across the vale to the estuary.

Food, transport and dogs

The Old Forge tea room by the green opens Wednesday to Sunday. Bus 42 from the market town stops outside the hall every two hours. Sheep graze the upper slopes from March to June, so keep dogs on a lead above the cattle grid.

When to go

Bluebells fill Hanger Wood in late April. For a shorter option, the 3 km riverside path to Combe Weir is flat and buggy friendly.

meta description: The Brackenmoor tarn circuit: 12 km, 450 m of ascent, with parking, cafés and dog advice.
body:
Planning a walk near Brackenmoor? Sample Outdoors has put together this guide to walking in and around the area, with routes for every ability. Before you set off, check the weather forecast, wear supportive footwear and carry water, a map and a charged phone.

The Brackenmoor tarn circuit

The Brackenmoor tarn circuit is a 12 km circular walk with 450 metres of ascent, starting from the forestry lay-by at Gallows Gate, which fills by 9am at weekends. Open moorland with a peaty path marked by wooden posts; navigation is tricky in mist. Highlights include two upland tarns, a Bronze Age cairn and nesting curlews in spring.

Food, transport and dogs

there is no café on the route, so carry food; the Moorcock Inn serves lunch back at the road end. There is no public transport to the start. Ground-nesting birds mean dogs must be on leads from March to July.

When to go

Heather turns the moor purple in August. A compass bearing from the second tarn back to the posts is worth knowing before you go.

The Ridge and reservoir walk

The Ridge and reservoir walk is a 7.2 km circular walk with 240 metres of ascent, starting from the reservoir car park off the B-road, free with a small charge for the toilets. A tarmac dam track, then a well-made ridge path with one short scramble at Knuckle Rock. Highlights include the Victorian valve tower and long views over three counties on clear days.

Food, transport and dogs

The water company kiosk sells hot drinks at weekends. The nearest station is four miles away; taxis need booking. Dogs are welcome but swimming in the reservoir is not allowed.

When to go

The ridge is exposed and very windy in winter. Families can turn back at the valve tower for a level 3 km out-and-back.

The Dunholt castle and canal walk

The Dunholt castle and canal walk is a 6 km circular walk with 90 metres of ascent, starting from the canal basin, where there is on-street parking on Wharf Road. A level towpath, then field paths with three stiles up to the castle mound. Highlights include the castle earthworks, a flight of five locks and kingfishers along the canal.

Food, transport and dogs

The Lock Keeper's Cottage café sits halfway along the towpath. Dunholt station is a five-minute walk from the basin. The stiles have dog gates, though the castle field holds cattle in summer.

When to go

The towpath is muddy from November to February. Step-free walkers can stay on the towpath and skip the castle mound.

The Elderford stepping stones walk

The Elderford stepping stones walk is a 5.4 km circular walk with 120 metres of ascent, starting from the free car park behind St Anne's church. Woodland paths with tree roots and a crossing of 22 stepping stones. Highlights include the stepping stones, an old packhorse bridge and a wild garlic wood.

Food, transport and dogs

The Ford Bakery does takeaway pasties and coffee. Bus 7 runs hourly from the county town on weekdays. Most dogs manage the stepping stones; there is a footbridge alternative 200 metres upstream.

When to go

After heavy rain the stones are underwater, so use the footbridge. The wild garlic smell in May is a highlight of this route.

The Gorsedale waterfalls trail

The Gorsedale waterfalls trail is a 4.8 km circular walk with 180 metres of ascent, starting from the National Trust car park, free for members. A stepped gorge path that is slippery when wet, with handrails at the steepest parts. Highlights include four waterfalls, the largest dropping about 15 metres into a plunge pool.

Food, transport and dogs

A seasonal kiosk at the car park opens Easter to October. A summer shuttle bus runs from the town at weekends. Dogs on leads; the steps are hard for older dogs.

When to go

The falls are most impressive after a wet spell in autumn. Wear boots with good grip: the gorge rocks stay damp all year.

The Hollinsby coast and dunes walk

The Hollinsby coast and dunes walk is a 8.3 km circular walk with 60 metres of ascent, starting from the beach car park at the end of Shore Road (charges April to September). Firm sand at low tide, then a boardwalk through the dunes. Highlights include a seal colony on the sandbar, a wartime pillbox and natterjack toad ponds.

Food, transport and dogs

The Dune Hut serves fish and chips in summer. The coast bus stops at the top of Shore Road. Dogs are banned from the main beach from May to September; use the dune path instead.

When to go

Check the tide times: the sandbar section is cut off two hours either side of high tide. Keep at least 50 metres from the seals, especially in the pupping season.

The Ivydown hill fort walk

The Ivydown hill fort walk is a 6.7 km circular walk with 210 metres of ascent, starting from the lay-by on the downs road, room for about ten cars. Chalk grassland on a steady climb, with flint paths that are slippery in frost. Highlights include the double ramparts of the hill fort, chalkhill blue butterflies and a dew pond.

The farm shop at the foot of the down has a small café. There is no bus; the nearest station is 6 km away. Cattle graze inside the ramparts from May to October.

When to go

Wild orchids flower on the ramparts in June. An information board at the dew pond explains how the ramparts were built.

title: The three peaks of the vale: a 24 km challenge route | Sample Outdoors
h1: The three peaks of the vale: a 24 km challenge route
meta description: The three peaks of the vale: a 24 km challenge route
body:
Overview

This long-distance challenge links Ashcombe Beacon, Thornby Fell and Ivydown in a single day. Allow nine to eleven hours and start before 7am in summer.

Planning

There are two resupply points: the Moorcock Inn at 9 km and the farm shop below Ivydown at 17 km. Water is not available on the tops. Leave a route plan with someone at home and carry a head torch even in June, because the final descent through Hanger Wood is dark early.

Kit

Lightweight boots or trail shoes with grip, a waterproof jacket with taped seams, poles for the descents and at least two litres of water. The moorland section needs a map and compass; phone signal drops out between the first and second peak.

Getting back

The route ends at Ivydown, six kilometres from the start; book a taxi in advance or leave a second car at the farm shop.

body:
How we chose these walks

Every walk here is under 5 km, has toilets at the start, and avoids roads and cliff edges. We noted where buggies can go and where they cannot.

The walks

Combe Weir riverside path (3 km, buggy friendly, ducks and a playground at the end). Larkhollow family trail (3 km, a wooden play area and a stream for paddling). Saltmere lagoon to the bird hide (2.5 km each way, flat boardwalk). Gorsedale lower falls (1.5 km, steps, not for buggies).

Tips

Bring a spare layer for each child, plenty of snacks and a small first aid kit. Start with the shortest walk and let children set the pace; most families find 3 km takes about an hour and a half with stops.

title: Winter walking on the moors: what changes | Sample Outdoors
h1: Winter walking on the moors: what changes
meta description: Winter walking on the moors: what changes
body:
Shorter days

In December there are fewer than eight hours of usable light. Plan to be off the tops by 3pm and carry a head torch with spare batteries.

Ground conditions

Peat paths freeze hard and then turn to deep mud in a thaw. Flagstones and boardwalks become slippery with frost; microspikes help on icy sections but are not a substitute for crampons on steep snow.

Layers

Wind on the ridges makes it feel much colder than the valley forecast. Pack a warm hat, gloves, a spare insulated layer and a flask. Mountain weather forecasts give wind speeds on the summits; check them, not just the town forecast.

Navigation

Snow hides paths and posts, so practise with a map and compass on a clear day before relying on it in poor visibility.

title: Dog-friendly routes around the vale | Sample Outdoors
meta description: Dog-friendly routes around the vale
body:
What makes a route dog friendly

We looked for routes with water to drink, few stiles, little livestock and pubs or cafés that welcome dogs.

Our picks

Larkhollow beech woods: shade and streams all the way. Dunholt canal towpath: flat, with dog gates on the stiles. Coldwater Ridge: open views, but no swimming in the reservoir.

Seasonal rules

Brackenmoor and Ivydown have ground-nesting birds or grazing cattle in spring and summer, so leads are required. Hollinsby beach bans dogs from May to September; the dune path is the alternative.

Ticks

Bracken and long grass carry ticks from spring to autumn. Check your dog and yourself after each walk and remove ticks with a tick hook.
